cards.front: What are the four main layers of the Earth, from the centre outwards?
cards.answer: Inner core / Outer core / Mantle / Crust

cards.front: What are the three main factors that determine how dangerous a natural hazard is?
cards.answer: Scale of the hazard / Wealth of the country / Population size and proximity

cards.front: How do convection currents in the mantle make tectonic plates move?
cards.answer: Heat from the core makes magma in the mantle rise, cool and sink in circular currents, which drag the plates along with them.

cards.front: Why do earthquakes and volcanoes occur in lines rather than being spread randomly across the world?
cards.answer: They occur along the edges of tectonic plates, which meet in clear lines that mark the plate boundaries.

cards.front: What are the four types of plate boundary?
cards.answer: Constructive / Destructive / Conservative / Collision

cards.front: Why do conservative plate boundaries produce earthquakes even though they have no volcanoes?
cards.answer: Friction between the sliding plates builds up pressure, which causes an earthquake when it is suddenly released.

cards.front: Why are there no volcanoes at a collision plate boundary?
cards.answer: Neither plate is subducted or melted, because both plates are made of continental crust with the same density.

cards.front: Why was Haiti's government unable to coordinate the relief effort after the 2010 earthquake?
cards.answer: Its own government buildings and infrastructure had been destroyed by the earthquake.

cards.front: Why did New Zealand recover much faster than Haiti after their earthquakes?
cards.answer: New Zealand's wealth let it mobilise help quickly, repair infrastructure within months, and use insurance to fund rebuilding.

title: Managing Tectonic Hazards: The Three Ps

cards.front: What are the Three Ps for managing tectonic hazards?
cards.answer: Prediction / Protection / Planning

cards.front: Why can scientists often give more warning before a volcanic eruption than before an earthquake?
cards.answer: Rising magma produces measurable changes in ground shape, gas emissions and seismic activity that build up beforehand.

cards.front: Why is a seismometer warning of only 10-60 seconds still valuable during an earthquake?
cards.answer: It gives people just enough time to take protective action, like turning off gas or sheltering under furniture.

cards.front: What are the three global atmospheric circulation cells, from the equator to the poles?
cards.answer: Hadley Cell / Ferrel Cell / Polar Cell

cards.front: What are the four main hazards created by a tropical storm?
cards.answer: Damaging winds / Torrential rain / Storm surge / Flooding

cards.front: Why does the UK experience frequent rain and unsettled weather?
cards.answer: The UK sits near the edge of the Ferrel Cell, where rising air brings unsettled, rainy weather.

cards.front: Why do tropical storms weaken quickly after they move over land?
cards.answer: They lose their energy source, because a tropical storm's energy comes from the warm ocean beneath it.

cards.front: What are the three Ps used to reduce damage from a tropical storm?
cards.answer: Prediction / Protection / Planning

cards.front: Why did many people in the Philippines fail to evacuate or protect their homes before Typhoon Haiyan?
cards.answer: Many people could not afford to evacuate or protect their homes, because the Philippines is a newly emerging economy.

cards.front: Why is moving inland the best advice when a tropical storm is approaching the coast?
cards.answer: Tropical storms are powered by warm ocean water, so they lose energy and weaken once they move over land.

cards.front: Why does the confluence of the Derwent and Cocker rivers increase flood risk in Cockermouth?
cards.answer: The two rivers meet at a confluence there, which doubles the volume of water flowing through the town.

cards.front: Why did the floodwater in Cockermouth pose a serious health risk?
cards.answer: Sewage contamination polluted the floodwater, so anything it touched had to be destroyed to prevent disease.

cards.front: What are the four natural factors that have driven climate change throughout Earth's history?
cards.answer: Volcanic activity / Orbital changes (Milankovitch cycles) / Sunspot activity / Ice reflection (albedo effect)

cards.front: What are the three main human causes of climate change?
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels / Agriculture / Deforestation

cards.front: Why does melting ice accelerate global warming?
cards.answer: Melting ice exposes darker land or ocean, which absorbs more heat than reflective ice did, speeding up warming.

cards.front: Why do population growth and rising wealth make climate change worse?
cards.answer: More people and greater wealth increase fossil fuel use, farming, deforestation and consumption, all of which raise emissions.

cards.front: What are the three stores in an ecosystem's nutrient cycle?
cards.answer: Soil / Biomass (living plants and animals) / Litter (dead organic material)

cards.front: Why is so little energy passed from one trophic level to the next in a food chain?
cards.answer: Energy is lost at each stage through respiration, movement, excretion and uneaten body parts, so only about 10% passes on.

cards.front: Why is the brown earth soil in Epping Forest so fertile?
cards.answer: Decomposing leaves enrich it with nutrients, and earthworms mix these nutrients through the different soil layers.

cards.front: What are the five layers of a tropical rainforest, from the tallest to the forest floor?
cards.answer: Emergent layer / Canopy / Under-canopy / Shrub layer / Forest floor

cards.front: What are the four plant adaptations described for surviving in a tropical rainforest?
cards.answer: Drip tip leaves / Buttress roots / Smooth bark / Lianas

cards.front: Why do leaf-cutter ants carry cut leaves back to their nest rather than eating them straight away?
cards.answer: The leaves are left to decompose in the nest and grow a fungus, which the ants then eat.

cards.front: Why does rainforest soil become infertile so quickly after deforestation?
cards.answer: Without trees to absorb nutrients, rapid leaching strips the humus layer and soil erosion accelerates.

cards.front: What are the four main causes of deforestation in the Amazon?
cards.answer: Farming (agriculture) / Logging / Mineral extraction / Energy development (HEP)

cards.front: What are the six main strategies for sustainably managing tropical rainforests?
cards.answer: Selective logging / Replanting / International agreements / Conservation / Education / Ecotourism

cards.front: Why do debt-for-nature swaps encourage poorer countries to protect their rainforests?
cards.answer: Richer nations or charities cancel part of the country's debt in exchange for a promise to protect the forest.

cards.front: Why is selective logging difficult and time-consuming to carry out?
cards.answer: It is hard to access individual, fully grown trees scattered deep within the forest.

cards.front: What are the four cactus adaptations described for surviving in hot deserts?
cards.answer: Spines instead of leaves / Fleshy stems / Thick, waxy skin / Long and shallow roots

cards.front: What are the five fennec fox adaptations described for surviving in the desert?
cards.answer: Large, bat-like ears / Thick fur on feet / Long, thick hair / Light-coloured fur / Nocturnal behaviour

cards.front: Why do camels rarely sweat, even in extreme desert heat?
cards.answer: Not sweating helps the camel conserve water for long periods in the extreme heat.

cards.front: Why do many desert plants have both deep and shallow roots?
cards.answer: Deep roots reach underground water, while shallow, widespread roots catch rain near the surface.

cards.front: What are the four main development opportunities in the Sahara Desert?
cards.answer: Solar energy / Mining and mineral extraction / Tourism / Farming

cards.front: What are the three main strategies used to manage desertification?
cards.answer: Appropriate (intermediate) technology / Bunds (magic stones) / Afforestation (Great Green Wall)

cards.front: Why does population growth increase the risk of desertification?
cards.answer: More people increase demand for food, farmland and fuelwood, pushing farming onto marginal, less suitable land.

cards.front: Why does cutting down trees for firewood lead to soil erosion?
cards.answer: Removing trees leaves the soil exposed, so it is easily washed or blown away.

cards.front: What are the three types of weathering that attack coastal rock?
cards.answer: Mechanical (physical) weathering / Chemical weathering / Biological weathering

cards.front: What are the four main types of mass movement at the coast?
cards.answer: Rockfall / Landslide (sliding) / Slumping (rotational slip) / Mudflow

cards.front: Why do waves usually approach UK beaches at an angle, causing longshore drift?
cards.answer: They are pushed by the prevailing wind, which blows from the south-west in the UK.

cards.front: Why do sheltered bays typically develop beaches?
cards.answer: Waves entering a bay spread out and lose energy, so they can no longer carry sediment and deposit it instead.

cards.front: What are the five stages of headland erosion, from crack to stump?
cards.answer: Crack / Cave / Arch / Stack / Stump

cards.front: Why does Lulworth Cove have a near-circular shape?
cards.answer: Waves broke through the hard limestone at the front, then rapidly eroded the softer clay behind it.

cards.front: Why do sand dunes become more stable once marram grass colonises them?
cards.answer: Marram grass roots bind the sand grains together, holding the dune in place.

title: Coastal Management & Lyme Regis Case Study

cards.front: What five management strategies were used at Lyme Regis?
cards.answer: New sea wall and promenade / Stone groynes / Rock armour / Beach nourishment / Cliff stabilisation

cards.front: What are the four hard engineering methods described for coastal management?
cards.answer: Sea walls / Groynes / Rock armour (rip-rap) / Gabions

cards.front: Why does rock armour reduce the force of a wave's backwash?
cards.answer: Gaps between the boulders let water percolate through, which absorbs wave energy and weakens the backwash.

cards.front: Why does Lyme Regis use several coastal management strategies together rather than just one?
cards.answer: Each strategy tackles a different threat; for example, sea walls reflect waves but do not replace lost beach material.

cards.front: What are the six key features of a drainage basin?
cards.answer: Source / Mouth / Tributary / Confluence / Watershed / River channel

cards.front: What are the three sections of a river's long profile, from source to mouth?
cards.answer: Upper course / Middle course / Lower course

cards.front: Why is vertical erosion dominant in a river's upper course?
cards.answer: The gradient is steep there, giving the river plenty of energy to cut downward into its bed.

cards.front: Why does lateral erosion become more important in a river's middle and lower course?
cards.answer: As the gradient becomes gentler, the river erodes sideways into its banks instead of downwards, widening the valley.

cards.front: What are the four stages of waterfall formation, from erosion to retreat?
cards.answer: Abrasion wears away the soft rock / Hard rock is undercut, forming an overhang / The overhang collapses into the plunge pool / The waterfall retreats upstream
items: Abrasion wears away the soft rock
Hard rock is undercut, forming an overhang
The overhang collapses into the plunge pool

cards.front: What are the four stages of oxbow lake formation?
cards.answer: The neck between bends narrows / Flood water cuts across the neck / The river returns to its channel / The loop is cut off, forming a lake
items: Flood water cuts across the neck
The river returns to its channel
The loop is cut off, forming a lake

cards.front: Why do estuaries contain such large amounts of deposited sediment?
cards.answer: The land is flat, so the river moves slowly and has little energy left to carry material onward.

cards.front: Why does a river's flood plain become more fertile over time?
cards.answer: Each flood deposits a fresh layer of sediment across the flood plain, gradually making it higher and more fertile.

cards.front: What are the three key physical factors that affect flood risk?
cards.answer: Rainfall / Geology / Relief (shape of the land)

cards.front: What are the four ways water can be stored in a drainage basin?
cards.answer: Interception (on trees) / Surface storage (lakes, reservoirs) / Soil moisture / Groundwater

cards.front: Why can sudden heavy summer rain cause flooding even when the ground looks dry?
cards.answer: Dry, baked soil is hard for water to infiltrate, so the rain runs off the surface instead.

cards.front: Why are valleys at the foot of steep mountains especially vulnerable to flooding?
cards.answer: They collect surface runoff draining quickly downhill from a large surrounding area of steep land.

cards.front: What are the three categories of impact evaluated for the River Tees flood management scheme?
cards.answer: Social impacts / Economic impacts / Environmental impacts

cards.front: What are the four hard engineering strategies described for managing river floods?
cards.answer: Dams and reservoirs / Embankments / Channel straightening / Flood relief channels

cards.front: Why can flooding be worse if an embankment is breached?
cards.answer: Water becomes trapped behind the raised bank, because the embankment blocks its route back to the river.

cards.front: Why can channel straightening increase flood risk further downstream?
cards.answer: Water flows through the straightened section much faster, so more water arrives downstream sooner, increasing the flood risk there.

cards.front: What are the five push factors that drive rural-urban migration, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Drought and climate hazards / Subsistence farming with no surplus / Few doctors or hospitals / Only basic education available / Isolation with poor infrastructure

cards.front: What are the six pull factors that attract people to cities, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Better paid jobs / Better education / Better healthcare and clean water / Improved transport and communication / More entertainment and social life / Friends and family already there

cards.front: Why do healthcare and sanitation improvements in cities add to population growth beyond migration?
cards.answer: They reduce the death rate and infant mortality, so natural increase adds further to the growing population.

cards.front: Why are most of the world's newest megacities emerging in LICs and NEEs rather than HICs?
cards.answer: They have fast rural-urban migration and high natural increase, while HICs have already urbanised and grow much more slowly.

cards.front: At what three levels can Rio de Janeiro's importance be understood?
cards.answer: Regional / National / International

cards.front: What are the four types of social opportunity created by Rio's growth, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Education / Healthcare / Water supply / Energy

cards.front: How does the multiplier effect create extra jobs in Rio's economy?
cards.answer: New investment creates jobs, which leads to more spending, which in turn creates even more jobs.

cards.front: Why do people still move to Rio for informal-sector jobs even though they pay little?
cards.answer: Informal jobs in Rio pay little, but still earn more than subsistence farming does in rural areas.

cards.front: What are the three environmental challenges described for Rio, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Traffic congestion and air pollution / Waste disposal / Water pollution

cards.front: What are the four social challenges described for Rio, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Lack of clean water and sanitation / Poor health and energy supply / Low education and high unemployment / Crime
items: Lack of clean water and sanitation

cards.front: Why has traffic congestion worsened in Rio in the last decade?
cards.answer: Car numbers have risen 40%, and high crime levels make many people choose to drive instead of using public transport.

cards.front: Why does pollution in Guanabara Bay threaten Rio's tourism industry?
cards.answer: It harms wildlife and reduces fish populations, which could damage tourism at famous beaches like Copacabana.

cards.front: What are the three main approaches used in the Favela Bairro scheme?
cards.answer: Site and service schemes / Self-help schemes / Pacification (UPPs)

cards.front: What are the four areas in which Curitiba made itself sustainable?
cards.answer: Transport / Parks and green space / Waste management / Housing

cards.front: Why did property values rise in favelas after Pacifying Police Units reduced crime?
cards.answer: As crime fell, residents felt safer and outside investors became willing to invest in the area.

cards.front: Why does Curitiba's Green Exchange programme work well in narrow-streeted informal settlements?
cards.answer: Refuse vehicles cannot reach these narrow streets, so residents bring their own waste to collection points instead.

cards.front: For what four things is Liverpool globally recognised, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Music (the Beatles) / Football (Liverpool FC and Everton FC) / Education (three universities) / Tourism (67 million visitors a year)

cards.front: By what four types of transport is Liverpool well connected?
cards.answer: Road / Rail / Sea / Air

cards.front: Why did Liverpool's location make it such an important global trading port?
cards.answer: Its sheltered estuary gave it a natural deep-water harbour, and its west-coast position made it a gateway to the Atlantic.

cards.front: Why has tourism played an important role in Liverpool's regeneration?
cards.answer: It has helped revive the city's economy since traditional port industries went into decline in the mid-20th century.

cards.front: What are the five areas of social deprivation described for Liverpool, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Housing / Education / Outward migration / Health / Waste disposal

cards.front: What are the three migrant communities described as shaping Liverpool's character?
cards.answer: Irish / Chinese / Afro-Caribbean

cards.front: Why did the negative multiplier effect make it so hard for Liverpool to recover from decline?
cards.answer: Factory closures led people to leave, buildings became derelict, crime rose, and investors were put off creating new jobs.

cards.front: Why did tensions sometimes arise between settled communities and new migrants in Liverpool?
cards.answer: Competition for jobs was fierce during periods of high unemployment, creating tension between settled residents and new arrivals.

cards.front: What are the three categories of benefit Chavasse Park provides, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Environmental benefits / Social benefits / Economic benefits

cards.front: What are the five reasons urban greening is important for cities, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Reduces pollution / Regulates temperature (heat island) / Provides recreational space / Supports small ecosystems / Makes cities more attractive

cards.front: Why are international students especially valuable to Liverpool's local economy?
cards.answer: Their higher tuition fees and living costs bring extra money into the local economy from outside the UK.

cards.front: Why did the Capital of Culture award keep attracting investment to Liverpool long after 2008?
cards.answer: It rebranded Liverpool's image, moving it away from its negative 1980s reputation and showing culture could drive regeneration.

cards.front: What are the four positives of urban sprawl and commuter settlements, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: New construction jobs / New social facilities / Improved transport infrastructure / Attractive homes near rural areas

cards.front: What are the four negatives of urban sprawl and commuter settlements, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Loss of green space and biodiversity / Increased flood risk / Increased traffic congestion / Rising house prices exclude locals
items: Loss of green space and biodiversity

cards.front: Why is building on brownfield land like the Liverpool ONE site better for the environment than building on greenfield land?
cards.answer: It reuses land that was already developed, so no new green space or countryside is lost.

cards.front: Why is improving home insulation a key part of Liverpool's plan to cut carbon emissions?
cards.answer: Around 40% of the city's carbon emissions come from homes, so insulating them cuts emissions significantly.

cards.front: What are the three broad groups geographers classify countries into based on wealth?
cards.answer: High Income Countries (HICs) / Newly Emerging Economies (NEEs) / Low Income Countries (LICs)

cards.front: What are the five stages of the Demographic Transition Model, in order?
cards.answer: Stage 1: High fluctuating / Stage 2: Early expanding / Stage 3: Late expanding / Stage 4: Low fluctuating / Stage 5: Decline

cards.front: Why can a country's national life expectancy figure hide big inequalities within that country?
cards.answer: A single national average can hide large regional differences, such as between north-east England and London.

cards.front: Why does population grow rapidly in Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model?
cards.answer: Death rates fall due to better food, water and healthcare, but birth rates stay high, so population grows fast.

cards.front: What are the four physical causes of uneven development described in the lesson?
cards.answer: Being landlocked / Tropical diseases (e.g. malaria) / Poor climate and soil / Natural hazards

cards.front: What are the five consequences of uneven development described in the lesson?
cards.answer: Health / Wealth inequality / International migration / Remittances / Brain drain

cards.front: Why do trading blocs such as the EU tend to benefit HICs more than LICs?
cards.answer: LICs are rarely members, so they pay full tariffs on goods while competing against each other on raw material prices.

cards.front: Why does a country hosting a TNC like Shell often miss out on much of the wealth it generates?
cards.answer: Most profits flow back to the HIC where the company is headquartered, rather than staying in the host country.

title: Reducing the Development Gap & Tourism in Kenya

cards.front: What are the three forms international aid can take, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Bilateral aid / Multilateral aid / NGO aid

cards.front: What are the four ways tourism helps reduce the development gap in Kenya, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Jobs / Foreign currency / Multiplier effect / Skills development

cards.front: Why can FDI sometimes fail to benefit local workers and the host economy long-term?
cards.answer: TNCs may relocate to where labour is cheaper and profits often flow back to the HIC headquarters.

cards.front: Why is relying heavily on tourism risky for a country's development, as shown by Kenya?
cards.answer: Tourism is vulnerable to shocks like terrorism or disease, and when visitor numbers drop, jobs and revenue fall.

cards.front: At what three scales does India's importance operate, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: National / Regional / Global

cards.front: What four factors drove India's rapid population growth, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Families wanting many children / Limited family planning and contraception / Falling death rates from better healthcare / High child death rate encouraged more
items: Falling death rates from better healthcare
High child death rate encouraged more

cards.front: Why is India's location important for international trade?
cards.answer: Its central position connects trade routes between Europe, Africa and East Asia, and its long coastline gives ships easy port access.

cards.front: Why does the legacy of partition still cause conflict in the Kashmir region today?
cards.answer: Partition divided people by religion imperfectly, leaving lasting tension between India and Pakistan that still causes conflict in Kashmir.

cards.front: What are the four employment sectors described by the Clark Fisher model?
cards.answer: Primary sector / Secondary sector / Tertiary sector / Quaternary sector

cards.front: What are the five reasons given for why Hyundai chose to set up in India?
cards.answer: Large, low-wage workforce / Widely spoken English / Existing car factories / Central global location / Supportive government policies

cards.front: Why is it beneficial for India to import cheap raw materials and export finished products?
cards.answer: Turning cheaper raw materials into finished products for export adds greater value to the economy.

cards.front: Why does economic leakage reduce the benefits India gains from hosting TNCs like Hyundai?
cards.answer: Profits are sent back to the home country instead of being reinvested locally, so India gets less tax revenue and investment.

cards.front: What four types of aid does the lesson describe?
cards.answer: Bilateral aid / Multilateral aid / Emergency aid / Development aid

cards.front: Why has rural poverty in India kept rising even as the national economy grows?
cards.answer: Rural areas lack the industrial development that creates formal jobs, so many people rely on low-paid farming instead.

cards.front: Why is Goa's GNI per capita so much higher than Bihar's?
cards.answer: Goa's high income is driven largely by tourism, which Bihar's economy lacks to the same degree.

cards.front: What are the four main stages of globalisation, in order?
cards.answer: Industrial Revolution (Stage 1) / Post-war period 1945-1989 (Stage 2) / Digital age 1989-2008 (Stage 3) / Modern knowledge economy 2008-present (Stage 4)

cards.front: What are the five advantages of globalisation for the UK economy, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Economic growth / Cheaper goods and services / High-value production / Foreign investment / Migration filling skills shortages

cards.front: Why did many UK state-owned industries close in the 1980s?
cards.answer: Ageing equipment and rising costs made them unprofitable, so the government closed mines and privatised industries.

cards.front: Why does outsourcing widen the pay gap between skilled and unskilled UK workers?
cards.answer: Low-skilled workers cannot negotiate better wages when their jobs can easily be outsourced to cheaper countries abroad.

title: Post-Industrial UK: Business Parks, Environment & Rural Change

cards.front: What are the four advantages of the Castle Cement works near Clitheroe, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Economic boost of £9 million a year / 750,000 tonnes of cement produced / Chimney filters trap pollutants / Habitat for birds, badgers and bats
items: Economic boost of £9 million a year
Habitat for birds, badgers and bats

cards.front: What are the four disadvantages of the Castle Cement works near Clitheroe, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Traffic congestion from lorries / Air pollution from works and lorries / Noise and dust from blasting / Unattractive landscape hurting tourism
items: Air pollution from works and lorries

cards.front: Why has the number of science and business parks grown in the UK?
cards.answer: Demand for high-tech products is rising, the UK has strong research universities, and business clusters boost each other's growth.

cards.front: Why does South Cambridgeshire's rapid growth create problems for the area?
cards.answer: High car ownership causes congestion, house prices become unaffordable, and commuters spend their money in the city instead.

title: The North-South Divide, Transport & the UK in the Wider World

cards.front: What are the four main links that connect the UK to the wider world, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Trade / Culture / Transport / Electronic communications

cards.front: What are the three strategies described for reducing the north-south divide?
cards.answer: The Northern Powerhouse / Devolving powers / Local Enterprise Partnerships and Enterprise Zones
items: Local Enterprise Partnerships and Enterprise Zones

cards.front: Why do critics say the Northern Powerhouse plan has not lived up to its aim?
cards.answer: Critics argue it has been too focused on Manchester, with funding for other cities left unclear.

cards.front: Why would expanding Heathrow with a third runway carry serious environmental costs?
cards.answer: Heathrow already emits the most CO2 of any UK airport, and expansion would worsen noise for a million people.

cards.front: What are the three main human factors driving rising global energy demand?
cards.answer: Population growth / Economic development / Modern technology

cards.front: What are the three physical factors that make energy supply harder to secure, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Geology / Climate / Environment

cards.front: Why does easy-to-find energy lead to higher demand for it?
cards.answer: Production increases and costs fall, and cheaper energy then encourages people to use more of it.

cards.front: Why does deep-sea drilling for oil and gas endanger marine ecosystems?
cards.answer: It risks oil spills and habitat destruction, which can seriously damage ocean life and ecosystems.

cards.front: What are the five impacts of energy insecurity described in the lesson?
cards.answer: Blackouts / Reduced industrial output / Reduced food production / Environmental damage / Conflict

cards.front: What are the four stages of how fracking extracts gas from shale rock?
cards.answer: A well is drilled to the shale / Water, sand and chemicals are injected / This creates fissures, releasing gas / Gas is piped away for use
items: A well is drilled to the shale
Water, sand and chemicals are injected
Gas is piped away for use

cards.front: Why are the effects of energy insecurity generally more severe in LICs than in HICs?
cards.answer: HICs can invest in alternatives and imports, but LICs often cannot, so blackouts, wood burning and food shortages hit harder.

cards.front: Why did the government impose a moratorium on fracking in the UK?
cards.answer: It could not predict how large the earthquakes triggered by fracking might become, so the risk was judged too great.

title: Sustainable Energy & the Nepal Micro-Hydro Case Study

cards.front: What are the four ways micro-hydro has changed communities in Nepal, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: New businesses e.g. the noodle factory / More children can attend school / Better medical equipment and vaccine storage / Homes gain lighting and communication technology
items: New businesses e.g. the noodle factory
Better medical equipment and vaccine storage
Homes gain lighting and communication technology

cards.front: What are the four ways schools and offices can save energy, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Biomass boilers instead of gas / Automatic lighting with motion sensors / Automatic ventilation / Rainwater collection for flushing toilets

cards.front: Why can't weather-dependent renewables like wind and solar fully replace fossil fuels yet?
cards.answer: They are weather-dependent and cannot provide the constant base load of energy that fossil fuels and nuclear can.

cards.front: Why does reducing household energy use also improve a country's energy security?
cards.answer: Lower household energy use means the country needs to import less energy from abroad.
